summary: Contains a revised specification of the Internet Stream Protocol version 2, a protocol for carrying real-time streams with resource reservation. It is experimental and is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: A reserved fast lane on the Internet for things such as live video, so the traffic isn't stuck behind everyone else.

questions: what is scmp stream control message protocol
subtitle: A connection-oriented companion to IP that reserves resources along a multicast tree for real-time audio and video streams.

tldr.problem: Real-time traffic such as digital audio and video needs data to arrive within its deadlines, which best-effort IP cannot promise.
tldr.mechanism: ST2+ builds one-way streams from an origin to one or more targets. A control protocol, SCMP, sets up the route and reserves resources hop by hop using a flow specification, and a thin 12-byte ST header then carries the data along the reserved path.
tldr.outcome: ST2+ is an Experimental revision of RFC 1190 and is now Historic. The IESG note says neither version is an Internet Standard or under consideration for that status, and that other approaches to resource reservation were under development in the IETF.

today: RFC 1819 is Historic and was Experimental when published. It obsoletes RFC 1190, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its own IESG note says that neither version is an Internet Standard or under consideration for that status.

sections.title: What ST2+ Is and Where It Came From
sections.content:
The Internet Stream Protocol, Version 2 (ST2) is an experimental connection-oriented internetworking protocol that operates at the same layer as connectionless IP. It supports efficient delivery of data streams to single or multiple destinations for applications that require guaranteed quality of service (QoS), such as real-time digital audio and video and distributed simulation or gaming. It is an adjunct to IP, not a replacement. A typical application would use IP for ordinary data and control, and ST2 for the real-time data.

Like IP with ICMP, ST2 has two parts: ST for data transport, with a single simple PDU format built for fast forwarding, and SCMP, the Stream Control Message Protocol, for all control functions.

This document specifies the revised version, ST2+, which obsoletes RFC 1190. The first version of ST dates to the late 1970s and was used through the 1980s for experimental voice, video and simulation. The ST2+ effort aimed at clarifying, simplifying and removing errors from RFC 1190 to ensure interoperability. The IESG note stresses that neither version is an Internet Standard.
sections.plainLanguage: ST2+ is a second, special road built next to the normal Internet road, just for things like live video that cannot afford to be late.

sections.title: Streams, Agents and Supporting Modules
sections.content:
A stream is a one-way, simplex path from a sending origin to one or more receiving targets, shaped as a routing tree. The nodes are ST agents, the links are hops, and agents in the middle are intermediate agents or routers. Direction toward the targets is downstream and toward the origin is upstream.

ST2 uses a two-step model: first stream setup selects routes and reserves resources, then data transfer sends data over the established stream. Setup need not be real-time, while data transfer has stringent real-time requirements. The RFC defines the data protocol (ST), the setup protocol (SCMP) and a flow specification (the ST2+ FlowSpec). It assumes, but does not define, a routing function and a Local Resource Manager (LRM) at each host or router. The LRM performs admission control, computes the QoS the node can offer, reserves resources and enforces the QoS during data transfer.

Data transfer is deliberately unreliable. ST makes no attempt to recover from loss, since retransmitted real-time packets would often arrive too late, and reliability can be added by layers above. There is no fragmentation: the application segments data to the minimum MTU over all paths, and agents silently discard packets that are too long. Agents forward data only along paths whose next hop has explicitly accepted the stream.
sections.plainLanguage: First you book the lane and everyone on the road agrees to hold space for you. Only then do you start driving, and if a car gets lost nobody turns around to fetch it, because it would arrive too late anyway.

sections.title: The ST Data Header
sections.content:
ST and IP packets are told apart by the first four bits, the internetwork version number. IP uses 4 and ST has been assigned 5. The ST header is 12 bytes. It holds the ST version (the current ST2+ value is 3), the D-bit (1 for data packets, 0 for SCMP control messages), a 3-bit drop priority Pri from 0 (lowest) to 7, the total length, a header checksum, and the Stream ID (SID) made of a 16-bit unique id and the 32-bit IP address of the stream origin.

The SID is chosen at the origin so that it is globally unique, and each agent uses it as a quick lookup into its stream database for forwarding. The header checksum covers only the ST header, and data packets are not protected by an ST checksum, so they are delivered to the higher layer even with errors. During congestion, agents try to discard lower-priority packets first.

ST packets can also be encapsulated in IP, using IP Protocol number 5, to cross routers that do not support ST. Resource management is not possible across such segments, so the RFC suggests it only for portions of the network that are not a bottleneck.
sections.plainLanguage: Every packet wears a small name tag saying which stream it belongs to and how important it is, so the routers can sort it quickly and drop the least important ones first if things get crowded.

sections.title: Setting Up and Maintaining Streams with SCMP
sections.content:
SCMP uses a request-response model made reliable by retransmission after timeout. It defines 13 message types: ACCEPT, ACK, CHANGE, CONNECT, DISCONNECT, ERROR, HELLO, JOIN, JOIN-REJECT, NOTIFY, REFUSE, STATUS and STATUS-RESPONSE. Most requests must be acknowledged with an ACK, or an ERROR if the message has a syntax error.

To set up a stream, the origin allocates a SID, calls the routing function for next hops, asks the LRM to reserve resources, and sends a CONNECT to each next hop with the stream options, the FlowSpec and a target list. Each intermediate agent repeats this toward its own next hops. A target asks its application whether to accept and replies with ACCEPT or REFUSE, which travels back along the same path. The origin can later add or remove targets, change the FlowSpec with CHANGE, and tear the stream down.

Streams can be built sender-oriented, receiver-oriented (an empty stream that targets join) or mixed. The join authorization level in the CONNECT header sets whether targets may join, and whether the origin is told. Streams can also be placed in groups that share bandwidth, fate, route or subnet resources.

Agents detect neighbor failures with periodic HELLO messages, and a neighbor that restarts sets a Restarted-bit. If no valid HELLO arrives within a stream's RecoveryTimeout, the agent starts stream recovery, unless the origin chose the NoRecovery option.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender sends a booking request down the road. Each stop checks it has room and passes it on. When the last stop says yes, the answer rushes back and the lane is ready.

sections.title: The ST2+ Flow Specification
sections.content:
The FlowSpec carries the application's QoS requirements, and SCMP simply relays it to each LRM. A FlowSpec Version field says which format is used, and one stream uses a single format throughout. Version 0 is a Null FlowSpec that reserves nothing and exists for interoperability testing, and version 7 is the ST2+ FlowSpec. Implementations must support both.

The ST2+ FlowSpec expresses a QoS class, a precedence, and three basic parameters: message size, message rate and end-to-end delay. Each is given as a desired value and a limit, both set by the application, and an actual value that each LRM updates along the path, always bounded by the other two. If a node cannot stay within the limit, the stream cannot be built along that path.

Two QoS classes exist. QOS_PREDICTIVE allows the negotiated QoS to be violated for short intervals, reserves for the normal case, and must be supported. QOS_GUARANTEED is optional, never violates the negotiated QoS, and reserves for the worst case, which may overbook resources. Delay is measured in milliseconds, each agent adds at least 1 millisecond to the minimum delay, and the spread between maximum and minimum delay bounds the jitter.
sections.plainLanguage: You tell the road crew the speed you would love, the slowest you could live with, and then each stop writes down what it can really give you.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 1190
sections.content:
ST2+ aimed at simplification, clarification and codifying extensions already in implementations. Major differences from RFC 1190 include:

  • Hop identifiers (HIDs) were dropped in favor of globally unique Stream IDentifiers (SIDs).
  • Several stream options that no implementation used were removed: point-to-point, full-duplex, reverse charge and source route.
  • Subset implementations are no longer allowed, because they caused interoperability problems. Agents MUST implement the full protocol.
  • The ability of targets to request to join a stream was clarified, which helps streams scale to more participants.
  • Functions were separated more cleanly between ST and its supporting modules, and ST became independent of any particular FlowSpec.

The RFC says companies had products incorporating the protocol and that the BERKOM MMTS project used ST2 as its core protocol. It names no later deployments. The security section states that security issues are not discussed in the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors tidied up the rulebook: they threw out the rules nobody used and made everyone follow the whole book, so different teams' equipment would work together.

fields.name: ST
fields.desc: IP version number assigned to ST packets.

fields.name: D
fields.desc: 1 for data packets, 0 for SCMP control messages.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Must be zero with the flow specifications defined in this document.

fields.name: TotalBytes
fields.desc: Length in bytes of the entire ST packet including the header.

fields.name: HeaderChecksum
fields.desc: Checksum over the 12-byte ST header only.

fields.name: UniqueID
fields.desc: First part of the stream ID, locally unique at the origin.

fields.name: OriginIPAddress
fields.desc: Second part of the stream ID: 32-bit IP address of the origin.

messages.label: CONNECT
messages.note: Carries SID, options, FlowSpec and target list.

messages.label: CONNECT
messages.note: Target list narrowed to targets behind this hop.

messages.label: ACCEPT
messages.note: Includes the FlowSpec as accepted by the target.

messages.label: ACCEPT
messages.note: Sent back along the path the CONNECT traced.
